abstract_text: The shark fishery in Tanjungluar Lombok is one of the largest target shark fisheries in Indonesia. Fishers from this location mainly use surface longlines to catch pelagic sharks in the eastern Indian Ocean and adjacent waters. We used 20-year landing data to identify a possible decline in shark production due to the fishery. A daily basis catch data collection has been applied at Tanjungluar since 2014. This method provided more robust data and showed a stable catch pattern rather than using the sampling-based method applied earlier. In general, the total catch of sharks caught by the surface longline fisheries varied from around 300 individuals per month in the low season to more than 1000 individuals in the peak season. Two CITES-listed species, Carcharhinus falciformis, and Sphyrna lewini were dominant in the shark catch composition within the last two decades. The silky shark contributed around 20-60% of the total shark catch every month and showed an upward trend in the catch from 2005 to 2021. Interestingly, the implementation of either CITES mechanisms for the species or the national shark management program seemed to have no or less impact on this target fishery. We discussed some possible factors that may sustain the shark fishery.

title: CITES listings catalyze improved conservation prospects for sharks and rays in Bangladesh
abstract_text: Unsustainable catches, driven in part by illegal trade, threaten 70% of the 52 shark and 85% of 71 ray species confirmed or suspected to occur in Bangladesh. Reported landings of elasmobranchs from targeted and non-targeted small-scale and industrial fisheries have declined by half from 6,234 tons over the past two decades, while official exports of dried shark fins (combined with fish maw) spiked at over 2,000 tons between 2018-2020. There is growing concern about the harmful effects of overfishing these apex predators on local livelihoods, food security, and the national economy. CITES Appendix I and II listings of globally threatened sharks and rays have catalysed efforts to improve their conservation management in Bangladesh. In 2021, the Bangladesh Wildlife Act was amended to strictly protect species assessed as Critically Endangered or Endangered in the IUCN Red List and/or listed in CITES Appendix I, and to regulate possession and trade of species assessed as Vulnerable and/or listed in CITES Appendix II. Non-Detriment Finding assessments for four species/species groups, including 15 CITES Appendix II listed species, confirmed the need for improved interagency collaboration, monitoring, and trade transparency. These NDFs also highlighted the need to reduce non-target catches and domestic consumption and trade that will not necessarily be reduced through stricter regulations on international trade. Improved prospects for conservation management of elasmobranchs initiated through collaborative research, policy development, trainings, and educational outreach exemplify how CITES listings can catalyse institutional collaboration and empower government and non-government stakeholders to implement evidence-based conservation plans.

title: Overview of population demographics and habitat use of Mobula birostris in Aotearoa New Zealand

authors.affiliation: Manta Watch New Zealand Charitable Trust

abstract_text: Despite being fully protected in New Zealand waters since 2011, significant gaps remain in our knowledge of nearly all aspects of the oceanic manta’s (Mobula birostris) life history and ecology in New Zealand. This lack of data has hindered comprehensive conservation management planning for this globally threatened species; New Zealand’s Department of Conservation currently lists the species as “Data Deficient” in terms of its threat classification. A focused effort to better understand the New Zealand oceanic manta population over the past four years has resulted in a significant increase in knowledge of this species’ population dynamics and habitat use. Combining citizen science and dedicated research efforts, 618 verified sightings spanning the time period of 1994 to 2022 have been collated from New Zealand waters, including 103 ventral photographic IDs, comprising 71 females, 26 males and 6 individuals of unknown sex. Furthermore, preliminary findings from intensive field work conducted in 2021-22 suggests that New Zealand supports a significant and healthy population of M. birostris. Observations include extensive feeding aggregations of more than 50 individuals, sightings of heavily pregnant females feeding alongside subadult males (disc widths of 590cm and 300cm respectively) and numerous accounts of active courtship displays. Moreover, this population shows very low incidence of injuries (17 %). These initial findings support the hypothesis that M. birostris are resident for at least part of the year in Aotearoa New Zealand and likely reproducing there and suggest that this population may be critical in global conservation efforts to recover this endangered species.

abstract_text: The European Union and Seychelles tropical tuna purse seine fishery in the western Indian ocean incidentally captures three species of devil rays, the spinetail devil ray (Mobula mobular), the sicklefin devil ray (M. tarapacana), and the bentfin devil ray (M. thurstoni), all currently classified globally as Endangered by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature. We used observer data collected on tropical tuna purse seiners in 2010-2020 to analyse the relationship between the presence/absence of devil rays in the catches and the environmental conditions, the spatial and temporal variability of fishing locations, and fishing operational variables. We found that higher probability of capture was predicted in areas with relatively high chlorophyll-a concentrations, high sea surface temperature fronts, and low sea surface height. This may indicate that the presence of this planktivore species might be associated with mesoscale features resulting in elevated biomass of zooplankton. We also found higher probability of catching devil rays in sets on free-swimming schools of tuna than in sets on fish aggregating devices and smaller tuna catch sets. The spatial predictions identified two important areas (the Mascarene Plateau and central Indian Ridge) persistent throughout the year with higher probabilities of catching a devil ray, and two seasonal important areas (the western Arabian Sea and Equatorial Region) with higher catch probabilities during the winter monsoon regime (December-March). Information on the spatio-temporal and environmental preference of devil rays is crucial to support more holistic spatial management and conservation strategies to further reduce the bycatch of these species.
